title: The One Where Rachel Is Late

jokes.text: I'm coming soon to a theater near you. I'm in THX. I'm unsuitable for children!
jokes.setup: Joey is pointing at his WWI movie poster, trying to describe how impressive it is
jokes.punchline: He literally narrates movie marketing copy about himself as if those are personal achievements, including 'I'm in THX' and 'I'm unsuitable for children'
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey self-aggrandizement — he treats movie marketing language as personal bragging rights. 'I'm unsuitable for children' especially lands because it's so earnestly delivered. High character integration because only Joey's oblivious vanity makes this work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, check it out. It's a one-sheet from my movie. Look at that — Dolby Digital, 5.1 surround sound. I did that.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You did the surround sound?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I was in it. And it's rated PG-13 — I got it down from an R. Me. I convinced them.

jokes.text: I started that! / I thought I did! (re: Oscar buzz)
jokes.setup: Joey mentions his movie is 'generating Oscar buzz'
jokes.punchline: Both Joey and Chandler simultaneously claim credit for starting the Oscar buzz — implying the only people talking about it are these two friends in their apartment
jokes.explanation: Very economical joke. The simultaneous claim deflates the pomposity of 'Oscar buzz' by implying the entire conversation is a two-person echo chamber. Quick and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, I started the Oscar buzz for my movie!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That is a lie, and you know it.

jokes.text: I love taking limos when nobody died.
jokes.setup: Everyone is excited about taking a limo to Joey's premiere
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reveals her only prior limo experiences have been connected to death/funerals, delivered with cheerful sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Phoebe — dark backstory delivered with total innocence and joy. The line implies a genuinely sad life history while functioning as a celebration. Economy is excellent; six words do enormous character work.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A limo! Oh my God, we're taking a limo to the premiere!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I love limos. They're so fancy and sleek when you're going to something fun, but they're so dark and depressing when you're going to a funeral.

jokes.text: Rachel's heartfelt 'I loved these last 9 months' speech immediately deflated by the reveal she's still visibly pregnant and miserable
jokes.setup: Rachel gives a warm, touching speech about cherishing the pregnancy and being grateful to her friends
jokes.punchline: The camera/context immediately reveals she is still hugely pregnant and deeply uncomfortable — the speech is exposed as naive idealism about to be brutally reversed
jokes.explanation: Structural irony — the sweet speech sets up a tonal reversal. Works better on rewatch when you know what's coming. Not particularly quotable but functions well as a scene-setter.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I really miss being pregnant. It was such a magical time.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I felt so connected to my body, so alive.

jokes.text: That's right. Still no baby. (Chandler's aside to camera/audience)
jokes.setup: Rachel has just finished her speech about loving pregnancy; the audience expects the baby to arrive
jokes.punchline: Chandler dryly narrates the obvious — she's still pregnant — directly puncturing the narrative expectation
jokes.explanation: Chandler's dry narrator persona is perfectly deployed. Five words, maximum impact. The delivery is everything — deadpan acknowledgment of the comedic premise of the entire episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross?

jokes.text: You. / Like you haven't done enough. (Rachel glaring at Ross)
jokes.setup: Ross tries to offer Rachel his seat to be more comfortable
jokes.punchline: Rachel's withering 'You.' followed by 'Like you haven't done enough' — blaming Ross for her pregnancy discomfort with comic hostility
jokes.explanation: Classic pregnant-woman blaming the father joke, but elevated by Rachel's specific venom and the economy of 'You.' as a standalone line. The comedic pause before the second line is crucial.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, this is YOUR fault! You got me pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? How is this my fault?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You were trying to be helpful!

jokes.text: Rachel sees Ross and says simply: 'You.'
jokes.setup: Ross tries to offer Rachel his seat to be helpful
jokes.punchline: Rachel responds with a single loaded word — 'You.' — conveying complete blame and contempt for the man who got her pregnant
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word delivering a universe of meaning. The audience understands immediately that Rachel holds Ross entirely responsible for her discomfort. The pause and audience anticipation make this land hard.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? I wish you could help me. I really do. But unless you can turn into a seahorse, I don't think there's much you can do.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why a seahorse?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because the male seahorse is the one who gets pregnant. And I just think that would be fair.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, wouldn't that be great? We could just switch off every nine months? You carry it for a while, then I carry it...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: —and then we could just give it to Phoebe. I mean, she's always saying she wants to have kids. She could just take it.

jokes.text: I wish I were a sea horse. Because with sea horses, it's the male. They carry the babies. And then also, um, I'd be far away in the sea.
jokes.setup: Ross says he wishes he could do something to ease Rachel's misery
jokes.punchline: Ross's scientific escape fantasy — first the intellectually defensible reason (male seahorses carry young) then the honest second reason: he'd just be far away from Rachel
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The two-part structure is elegant: Ross first deploys his paleontologist/scientist persona (a factually correct seahorse observation that doubles as wish fulfillment), then the 'and then also, um, I'd be far away in the sea' demolishes the intellectual cover and reveals pure cowardice. The 'um' sells it as an afterthought Ross knows he shouldn't say. Only Ross — the nervous intellectual — could deliver this. Genuinely quotable and original.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know exactly how you feel. My back is killing me, and I'm so bloated.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh please. You ate a pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A big pizza!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, I'm carrying a human being inside of me. The only thing you're carrying is leftovers. Now get me some ice cream.

jokes.text: I know. I remember toward the end... / That's a great story. Tell it while you're getting me some iced tea.
jokes.setup: Monica starts to share a sympathetic story about her own experience (even though she was never pregnant — this is played as obliviousness)
jokes.punchline: Rachel weaponizes the pretense of interest to redirect Monica into servant duty
jokes.explanation: Sharp comedic misdirection. 'That's a great story' feigns engagement before the pivot reveals pure self-interest. Works because pregnant Rachel's entitlement is well-established and Monica walking away mid-story is a visual beat the audience can enjoy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Get out! Get out! GET OUT!

jokes.text: Oh, God, get out! Get out, get out, get out! (Rachel clearing the room)
jokes.setup: Rachel is visibly uncomfortable and fed up
jokes.punchline: She erupts and clears the entire room — everyone scrambles to leave instantly — the explosive release of her frustration played for laughs
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy built on Rachel's escalating misery. The visual of everyone scattering is the real joke. Not particularly original but serves the scene rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Did you have the baby yet?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, but if you ask me one more time, I'm gonna use this pregnancy weight to sit on you.

jokes.text: Do you want me to sit on you? Because I'll do it.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Rachel has had the baby yet — an obviously dumb question
jokes.punchline: Rachel threatens to weaponize her pregnant body as a threat, delivered with total seriousness
jokes.explanation: Very economical and character-specific. Rachel's combination of exhaustion and barely-contained aggression produces this wonderfully absurd threat. The deadpan 'Because I'll do it' sells it. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Estelle, what do you mean you sold them online? I asked you for six premiere tickets!

dialogue.speaker: Estelle
dialogue.line: Joey, do you know how much these are worth on eBay? I made a killing!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But those were for my friends! Now I'm sitting next to some random eBay user at my own premiere!

dialogue.speaker: Estelle
dialogue.line: That's not my problem, Joey. You want premium tickets, you pay premium prices.

jokes.text: Or you could do volunteer work. (Chandler's response to Rachel announcing she'll hang out with them)
jokes.setup: Rachel announces she was sent home and plans to hang out with the gang
jokes.punchline: Chandler's perfectly deadpan suggestion of volunteer work — implying she should find literally anything else to do
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler economy — four words that communicate an entire attitude. The randomness of 'volunteer work' as an alternative is what makes it funny rather than mean. Very much in Chandler's voice.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I only have one ticket to this thing.

dialogue.speaker: Estelle
dialogue.line: That's okay, I'll be your plus-one.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no - this is for someone special.

dialogue.speaker: Estelle
dialogue.line: I AM special, Joey.

jokes.text: I sold four on eBay. / You'll be sitting next to HotGuy372.
jokes.setup: Joey calls his agent Estelle, who was supposed to get him six premiere tickets
jokes.punchline: Estelle sold four of his tickets on eBay and can describe the buyer's username — betraying complete shamelessness about exploiting her own client
jokes.explanation: Estelle is a perfectly constructed side character and 'HotGuy372' is a great specific comic detail. The fact that she can recite the buyer's username implies she stalked the auction. Entirely character-driven and adds to Estelle's legacy of incompetent representation.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't want to go to the premiere.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: But I still want to be considered.

jokes.text: So that's it? I only get to bring one guest? / Yeah. What time do you want to pick me up?
jokes.setup: Joey is upset he only has one guest ticket
jokes.punchline: Estelle immediately assumes she is the one guest — with zero self-awareness about her conflict of interest
jokes.explanation: Perfect Estelle — the audacity of assuming she's the guest after selling his other tickets is a great character payoff. The pivot from complaint to pickup logistics is fast and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Does pregnancy make me invisible or something?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no. I can see you just fine. It's just that you're REALLY hard to miss right now.

jokes.text: I would still like to be acknowledged. / Because I'm pregnant, I'm invisible? / Definitely not invisible.
jokes.setup: Joey is deliberating over who to take to the premiere; Rachel was excluded because she said she couldn't attend
jokes.punchline: Rachel's complaint that she's invisible is hilariously undercut by her massive pregnant belly — 'Definitely not invisible' is the visual punchline
jokes.explanation: The 'Definitely not invisible' response is a perfect, clean visual gag. The setup (Rachel's complaint) makes the visual response land harder. Quick and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You snooze, you lose, man. That's the rule.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: He's not snoozing, he's teaching!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't care what you call it. Eyes closed, you're out.

jokes.text: If you pick me, I was planning on wearing a sequin dress out down to here.
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to influence Joey's decision about who to bring to the premiere
jokes.punchline: Monica attempts to use sex appeal as leverage on her gay-adjacent best friend — the competitive Monica personality driving her to weaponize a revealing dress
jokes.explanation: Decent character-driven moment showing Monica's win-at-all-costs personality. Joey's susceptibility to a revealing dress is well-established, making this land. Somewhat predictable but serves the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Just tell Joey to flip a coin. Heads, he comes with you. Tails, he stays home and practices his acting.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not helpful.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, but it's honest.

jokes.text: Pick whoever you want. Listen to your heart. What does it tell you? / Phoebe. Phoebe. Phoebe.
jokes.setup: Phoebe gives Joey a seemingly selfless, spiritual speech about listening to his heart
jokes.punchline: Joey's heart literally just chants Phoebe's name — the manipulation is completely transparent, her 'selfless' speech was entirely selfish
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's cosmic-guidance language being immediately exposed as pure self-interest is a good joke. The triple 'Phoebe. Phoebe. Phoebe.' rhythm works perfectly — like a prayer/chant that reveals her scheme.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You need to listen to your heart, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm listening.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's saying... Phoebe. Phoebe. Phoebe.

jokes.text: I think I want to take Chandler. / Phoebe, Phoebe, Phoebe. (Phoebe's repeated chanting, now ignored)
jokes.setup: Phoebe's heart-chanting scheme was supposed to make Joey pick her
jokes.punchline: Joey ignores it entirely and picks Chandler; Phoebe repeats the chant uselessly — the gag is that it completely failed
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback — Phoebe's manipulation scheme fails hilariously and she can only repeat the incantation with diminishing returns. The structure of the callback makes it funnier than the original joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: My heart's telling me to pick Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: My heart's telling me to pick Phoebe.

jokes.text: So you're never actually going to pay me back?
jokes.setup: Joey says paying for the premiere ticket is his way of paying Chandler back for years of financial support
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately realizes this means actual financial repayment is off the table forever
jokes.explanation: Very sharp and character-consistent. Chandler's anxiety about money and his long-suffering role as Joey's financial support system makes this hit. Perfect economy — the question says everything.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So by that logic, if you ever save my life, I owe you a Porsche.

jokes.text: I don't think you're comprehending just how slutty this dress is.
jokes.setup: Monica is upset Chandler was chosen over her despite her sequin dress offer
jokes.punchline: Monica doubles down by explicitly emphasizing the dress's sluttiness as a last-ditch argument — competitive Monica refusing to accept defeat
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Monica's argument — going from hinting at the dress to explicitly naming its sluttiness — is very Monica. The directness is funnier than the initial setup. Reasonably quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's a great dress, Joey. You'd look amazing in it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Thanks, but I'm gonna go with Chandler's suggestion.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, fine. But when you're out there looking like that, don't come crying to me. Actually, you know what? You will look good. You'll look so good that Chandler's gonna regret ever suggesting anything else.

jokes.text: Mon, maybe one of these guys wants to wear your dress. / I'm gonna go shave. Ahem. / Yeah, well, I'm gonna go, uh, spit.
jokes.setup: Phoebe makes a snarky suggestion that one of the guys could wear Monica's slutty dress; Joey and Chandler are caught off-guard by their own masculine insecurity
jokes.punchline: Both Joey and Chandler immediately retreat to performatively masculine activities (shaving, spitting) to restore their credibility
jokes.explanation: The masculine panic reaction is a solid visual gag. 'I'm gonna go spit' is the funnier of the two because it's so pointless as an activity. Chandler's 'Ahem' delivery probably sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, the guys could wear your slutty dress.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's not a slutty dress!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh honey, I've seen you in that dress. It's a slutty dress.

jokes.text: If I don't come out, it's because I've choked to death on the potpourri stink.
jokes.setup: Rachel announces she has to use the bathroom
jokes.punchline: She predicts her own death-by-potpourri with complete seriousness, implying Monica's bathroom is aggressively over-scented
jokes.explanation: Good specific detail — the potpourri is a Monica joke embedded in a Rachel complaint. The hyperbole of 'choked to death' is well-calibrated. Specific enough to be funny, universal enough to be relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I just want you to know that you mean a lot to me, man.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you mean a lot to me too.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We're like brothers.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We are brothers.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, this is getting too weird.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm gonna go.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, me too.

jokes.text: You hold her nose, I'll blow in her mouth and the kid'll just...out of her.
jokes.setup: The gang is discussing how to get Rachel's baby to come out; she's a week late
jokes.punchline: Chandler proposes an utterly absurd 'blowing a baby out' technique that conflates CPR with childbirth
jokes.explanation: Absurd and committed — Chandler's ridiculous quasi-medical logic is delivered with enough conviction to be funny. The '...out of her' trailing off suggests even he doesn't quite believe the physics. Slightly undermined by the gross factor.

jokes.text: One hundred thousand dollars. / How about 50 bucks? / I'll call Zurich and move some money.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Monica decide to bet on when Rachel will have her baby; Monica asks 'how much?'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe opens with $100,000; Monica counters with $50; Phoebe immediately accepts by offering to call Zurich — implying she has Swiss bank accounts while also being willing to drop to $50
jokes.explanation: Three-beat escalation that works beautifully. Phoebe's absurd opening bid (100K), Monica's pedestrian counter ($50), and then Phoebe's 'I'll call Zurich and move some money' — which treats the two amounts as equivalent — is excellent character comedy. 'I'll call Zurich' is a great specific comic detail that implies hidden Phoebe wealth mythology. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I bet she has the baby on Christmas Day!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, that's like a one in 365 chance.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I'm feeling lucky!

jokes.text: All right, whose turn is it to help me get up? / (beat) No one's here. / Oh, damn it.
jokes.setup: Rachel has been asking people to help her up throughout the episode; she calls for help
jokes.punchline: Everyone has fled the room (following her earlier 'get out!') — the visual of Rachel stranded alone, unable to get up unassisted, is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff — Rachel cleared the room in anger and now suffers the consequence. The irony is exactly earned. 'Oh, damn it.' is a great button. Mostly a physical/visual joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Whose turn is it to help me get up?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh right, I'm alone and stuck.

jokes.text: A little tall. Would you crouch down a bit so that I look taller?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are on the red carpet at the premiere; Joey asks how Chandler looks
jokes.punchline: Chandler, insecure about his height, asks Joey to crouch so Chandler appears taller in photos — revealing his own vanity at the glamorous event
jokes.explanation: Decent character-driven joke about Chandler's insecurity. The red carpet setting makes the vanity funnier. Not especially original but lands as a quick visual beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How do I look?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You look great!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, now make me look like that.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, Mon? Rach is here. And you're still pregnant. / Yeah, like 50 bucks.
jokes.setup: Monica and Phoebe bet that Rachel would have the baby today; Rachel shows up still visibly pregnant
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'Yeah, like 50 bucks' — she's already calculating her loss while Rachel is standing right there, treating Rachel's misery as a financial setback
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback that works on two levels: confirms the bet is still active and characterizes Monica as someone who, even when greeting a suffering friend, is doing financial calculations. Efficient and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You look great!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really? Thank you!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm gonna win so much money on you.

jokes.text: I have to go pee. Apparently this baby thinks my bladder is a squeeze toy.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just arrived and immediately needs to use the bathroom
jokes.punchline: The 'squeeze toy' metaphor — vivid, specific, and unexpectedly playful for how uncomfortable the situation is
jokes.explanation: Good comic metaphor — 'squeeze toy' is specific enough to be funny and vivid enough to get a visceral reaction. Well-constructed image that earns a solid laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I need to use the bathroom again. This baby is like a squeeze toy — every time I move, something comes out!

jokes.text: Damn it. Here's your 50 bucks. (Monica immediately hands over the money upon seeing Rachel return from bathroom still pregnant)
jokes.setup: Monica bet Rachel would have the baby today
jokes.punchline: Rachel's mere return from the bathroom without having given birth is enough to settle the bet — Monica pays up without even being asked
jokes.explanation: Quick and functional callback. Monica's immediate resignation ('Damn it') before Rachel even speaks is good character work. Gets a solid chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So Monica, how much did you lose?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Fifty dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wow. You know, I've always wondered... is it hard being so competitive?

jokes.text: That's interesting that you lost. Now, I forget, do you like to lose?
jokes.setup: Monica has just lost the bet and paid up
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's mock-solicitous question is a weaponized form of gloating — asking if Monica 'likes' to lose is a barely-veiled taunt
jokes.explanation: Phoebe being passive-aggressively smug while maintaining plausible innocence is very in-character. 'Now, I forget' feigns concern before the knife goes in. Good delivery-dependent joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hello, General Grant. I want you to camp in my area.

jokes.text: Until then, General Grant, why don't you set up camp right there?
jokes.setup: Monica agrees to double-or-nothing on Rachel having the baby tomorrow
jokes.punchline: Phoebe calls Monica 'General Grant' — likening her competitive strategy to military encampment — a weirdly specific and elevated historical insult
jokes.explanation: 'General Grant' is an unexpected and funny specific choice. The military metaphor applied to Monica's competitive betting is a good bit of absurdist elevation. Phoebe using a Civil War general's name feels right for her eccentric knowledge base.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So, we're not together, we're not broken up, we're in some kind of relationship limbo. I'm thinking of calling it 'The Rachel.'

jokes.text: People ask why we're not together. I just don't know what to tell them.
jokes.setup: Rachel is being difficult and demanding in the doctor's waiting area; Ross is exasperated
jokes.punchline: Ross's deadpan observation that people question why they're not a couple — when their current dynamic makes it painfully obvious
jokes.explanation: Excellent line — the irony is multi-layered. Ross and Rachel ARE together in a complicated sense (they made a baby), but the line works because their dysfunction is so obvious. Very quotable and audience-aware. High character integration because only Ross would frame his own failed relationship so wistfully.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, that outfit is completely inappropriate for the office.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Nobody make any sudden movements. We don't want to startle her.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Just back away slowly and nobody gets hurt.

jokes.text: No, I'm fine. / You don't think that's inappropriate? / What? / Good God, man. Don't anger it.
jokes.setup: Ross suggests Rachel change her outfit before the doctor's appointment; Rachel refuses
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'Good God, man. Don't anger it.' — treating Rachel's pregnant form as a dangerous creature to not provoke, escalating the joke beyond the fashion argument
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. 'Don't anger it' reframes pregnant Rachel as a wild animal — Chandler's survival instinct overriding his sympathy. The word 'it' is key: dehumanizing but not cruel, purely comedic. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Did you seriously just call me 'mommy'?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? It just came out!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It just came out? Ross, that's not okay. And honestly, it explains so much about you and your actual mother. No wonder she still does your laundry.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She does not—okay, she does, but that's different!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Is it though? Because right now you're looking at me the same way you look at her when she brings you soup.

jokes.text: Uh-uh, pal! Don't call me 'Mommy.' It's bad enough you call your own mother that.
jokes.setup: Ross placates Rachel by saying 'You're the mommy' — implying she gets final say
jokes.punchline: Rachel objects to 'Mommy,' then pivots to insulting Ross for calling his own mother 'Mommy' — a sudden attack from an unexpected angle
jokes.explanation: Classic comic pivot — the first complaint sets up the expectation of a maternal pride joke, then the second half attacks Ross's character from a totally different angle. The implication that grown Ross calls his mother 'Mommy' is a perfect character jab.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, that is weird. A grown man calling his mother 'Mommy.' I mean, at what point do you have to grow up and start calling her 'Ma' like the rest of us?

jokes.text: I'm actually with her on this one. (Chandler, re: the 'Mommy' insult)
jokes.setup: Rachel has insulted Ross for calling his mother 'Mommy'
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately sides with Rachel — confirming the 'Mommy' habit is real and he has opinions about it — delivered as if this has been a long-standing grievance
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — six words that confirm the joke's premise and add a new dimension (this is apparently a known Ross trait). Chandler's matter-of-fact siding against his best friend is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Were you always this annoying during pregnancy?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I wasn't pregnant, Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, that explains it.

jokes.text: When Carol was pregnant with Ben, were you this irritating?
jokes.setup: Rachel and Ross are sitting in the doctor's office; Ross is trying to be helpful
jokes.punchline: Rachel's direct question about whether Ross was always this annoying to pregnant women — it's an insult masquerading as a sincere inquiry
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Ross's history with Carol — the implication that he drove a previous pregnant partner equally crazy. Character-grounded insult with historical depth.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not trying to irritate you.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, you're doing a great job.

jokes.text: Well, then, you must have a natural talent for it.
jokes.setup: Ross protests that he's 'not trying to irritate' Rachel
jokes.punchline: Rachel counters that his irritating nature must be innate — a gift
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. Calling someone's irritating behavior a 'natural talent' is a well-turned phrase — it's insulting while maintaining a veneer of compliment. Fits Rachel's sharpness under pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, could you breathe any louder?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm just breathing normally.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, it's really annoying.

jokes.text: Seriously. Breathe louder, Ross. That's great.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel have agreed not to speak; Ross is breathing
jokes.punchline: Rachel's sarcastic commentary on Ross's breathing — implying even his involuntary bodily functions are annoying her — with the added sting of 'That's great'
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy moment — the hypersensitivity of attacking someone's breathing is both funny and relatable. 'That's great' as sarcastic punctuation elevates it. Good specific detail.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, come on, it's half you. It's going to be evil.

jokes.text: We should ask the doctor if she even knows how to deliver a baby that's half human, half pure evil!
jokes.setup: Rachel and Ross are in silent antagonism before the doctor arrives
jokes.punchline: Rachel's escalation to calling their unborn baby 'half pure evil' — projecting her anger at Ross onto their child
jokes.explanation: Funny escalation of Rachel's Ross-directed hostility. 'Half pure evil' is a great specific hyperbole. The doctor framing (asking an OB to handle a supernatural delivery) adds an absurdist layer.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, you have to be nice to the doctor. I mean, he's got a needle.

jokes.text: Hi, Dr. Long. How are you? / You're nice to her. / She has the drugs.
jokes.setup: Ross is surprised Rachel is suddenly pleasant to the doctor after being hostile to everyone
jokes.punchline: Rachel's explanation — 'She has the drugs' — is completely pragmatic and strips away any pretense of pleasantness being genuine
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy and character work. Three words explain everything about Rachel's strategic pleasantness. The pragmatic calculation is very funny and very Rachel. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: You could try having sex. It might induce labor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: With who?!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm right here.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know!

jokes.text: There are ways to help things along. / Do them!
jokes.setup: Doctor mentions there are ways to induce labor
jokes.punchline: Rachel's instant, explosive 'Do them!' — zero hesitation, complete desperation — before even knowing what they are
jokes.explanation: Two words that perfectly capture Rachel's desperation. The setup (the doctor's vague offer) + punchline (unconditional acceptance before details) is structurally clean. The speed of the response is what sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So in that scene where I'm storming the beach, did you see the part where I take out the machine gun nest?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, that was great. And then the giraffe showed up and you two danced the tango.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler, were you asleep?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No! ...Okay, yes.

jokes.text: And there's the one that's proved most effective: sex. / (long beat) You've got to be kidding me.
jokes.setup: Doctor lists home remedies (tea, castor oil, spicy food, walking) and Rachel eagerly agrees to all; doctor saves the last one
jokes.punchline: The final remedy is sex with Ross, the man Rachel has been treating with utter contempt all episode — the juxtaposition of her frantic 'do them all' attitude hitting this wall is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's structural highlights. The entire Rachel/Ross antagonism has been building toward this comedic payoff — the one thing she's been refusing to do with the man she hates right now is the medical prescription. 'You've got to be kidding me' is the perfect button. The audience sees it coming but the structure still delivers.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. A kangaroo? That was my idea!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, it wasn't.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yes, it was! I suggested it for that World War I movie!

jokes.text: Good job, Joe! Well done! Top-notch! / You liked it? You really liked it? / Well, which part exactly? / I loved the specifics. The specifics were the best part.
jokes.setup: The movie premiere is over; Chandler enthusiastically praises Joey's performance
jokes.punchline: Joey's probing questions expose that Chandler has no specific memory of the film — Chandler's increasingly vague praise ('I loved the specifics') reveals he may have slept through it
jokes.explanation: Nicely structured escalation. Each of Joey's probing questions creates another opportunity for Chandler's evasiveness to become more obvious. 'I loved the specifics' is a genuinely funny non-answer. The setup and payoff (falling asleep) is well-telegraphed but the specific lines are sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I just don't want you to feel pressured, you know? I mean, if you're not comfortable with it...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, I'm nine months pregnant. I think I can handle it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, but... what if it's weird? What if things are... different?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross, just tell her you're worried about the baby.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but also... I don't want to see the baby!

jokes.text: Hey, what about the scene with the kangaroo? Did you like that part? / I was surprised to see a kangaroo in a World War I epic.
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to catch Chandler in having not paid attention; asks about a specific scene
jokes.punchline: Chandler apparently went along with the kangaroo question and admitted surprise — which reveals he actually DID try to bluff rather than admit ignorance, making him look worse
jokes.explanation: Very funny specific detail — Chandler apparently confirmed a kangaroo scene rather than admit he was asleep. The absurdity of a kangaroo in a WWI film makes the reveal funnier. Good character moment for both: Joey's test, Chandler's failed bluff.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, what are we waiting for?

jokes.text: You fell asleep! There was no kangaroo! They didn't take any of my suggestions!
jokes.setup: Joey's kangaroo question was a trap; Chandler fell for it
jokes.punchline: Joey's reveal has three parts: (1) Chandler slept through the movie, (2) there was no kangaroo, (3) Joey had apparently lobbied for a kangaroo and been ignored — the third is the unexpected bonus reveal
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and strongest character moment. The triple reveal structure is excellent: (1) confirms the setup (Chandler slept), (2) validates the trap (no kangaroo), (3) adds a perfect absurdist surprise — Joey had ACTUAL kangaroo suggestions that were rejected. This is entirely Joey. The idea that he pitched kangaroo scenes for a WWI film and was upset they weren't included is perfect character comedy. Approaches the 8+ benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You should totally do it! I mean, Ross is a great guy, and you two have so much chemistry. Just go for it!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, I don't know...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, seriously! He's smart, he's funny, he's got that whole paleontologist thing going on. You'd be so lucky to sleep with him! I mean, I've seen him naked and—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, that's weird.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, go jump his bones! Do it tonight! In fact, I could probably get Chandler out of the apartment if you want to use my room!

jokes.text: Look, this guy fell asleep! He fell asleep too! Be mad at him! / Or call an ambulance!
jokes.setup: Joey is upset that Chandler fell asleep during his film and is trying to deflect blame
jokes.punchline: Joey points to other audience members who also fell asleep — then Chandler's 'Or call an ambulance' implies those people may not be sleeping but dead or unconscious
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. Joey's pathetic attempt to spread blame, Chandler's dark pivot to 'ambulance' are both funny. The implication that the film is so boring it may have caused medical emergencies is a good bit of dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? If you need to have sex to induce labor, I could... I could lend you Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, he owes me a favor!

jokes.text: It's been a really long time for you. I mean, women have needs. Do it. Get yours.
jokes.setup: Everyone is discussing whether Rachel should have sex with Ross to induce labor
jokes.punchline: Monica reduces the entire situation to Rachel's sexual needs and encourages her to use the medical recommendation as an excuse — 'Get yours' is hilariously crass
jokes.explanation: Monica being completely practical and crass about Rachel's situation is funny and character-consistent. 'Get yours' is an unexpectedly frank construction that gets a laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're betting money on Rachel's pregnancy? How could you do that? That's taking advantage of someone's misery for profit!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Says the guy who bet on whether Rachel would name the baby Emma or not.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's different!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How is that different?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I... I knew her!

jokes.text: If Ross isn't willing, he's not the only guy you can have sex with. You could borrow Chandler. Chandler is good.
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to find solutions for Rachel to have sex and induce labor
jokes.punchline: Monica casually offers to 'lend' her husband to Rachel for sex — as if Chandler is a household item — and her endorsement 'Chandler is good' is both a compliment and utterly bizarre
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The absurdist escalation of Monica casually offering Chandler as a sexual resource to her pregnant friend — with the product endorsement 'Chandler is good' — is simultaneously shocking, in-character (Monica's competitive practicality taken to extremes), and very funny. 'Chandler is good' has become a beloved Friends quote. High originality, strong structure, and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys were betting on whether I'm pregnant? That's... actually kind of genius. So what are the odds? Because I want in.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, no—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, I'm serious! If you're all going to profit off my potential misery, I should at least get a cut. What's my payout if I'm not pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not really how it works...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, it should. Honestly, this is the most attention my uterus has gotten in years. I'm not letting it go to waste.

jokes.text: While she's been going through this hell, you've been making money? / You're betting on your friend staying in this misery?
jokes.setup: It's revealed Monica and Phoebe have been betting on when Rachel will give birth
jokes.punchline: Ross and Phoebe's moral outrage — delivered with perfectly escalating horror at the callousness
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the next joke rather than a great joke itself. The indignation is played straight and while it has comic energy, it's primarily functional writing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you don't owe me anything.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no! I'm gonna pay you back, Chandler. Every penny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm serious. I always pay my debts.

jokes.text: I'll take that bet. / What? / I'm miserable. I may as well make some money out of it.
jokes.setup: Ross and Phoebe are morally outraged that Monica is betting on Rachel's suffering
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately volunteers to bet on herself — if she's going to be miserable, she might as well profit from it
jokes.explanation: Excellent subversion of expectations. The audience (and Ross/Phoebe) expect Rachel to be outraged; instead she's immediately practical and mercenary about her own misery. The logic is perfectly Rachel — if you can't fix the situation, monetize it. Great character integration and misdirection. Genuinely funny and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So I owe you... $1,200?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you could always do what you did with those headshots I paid for.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know, tell me you'll pay me back, then have a booger on your face the whole time.

jokes.text: Can I get some of that action? / I'm betting against all of you?
jokes.setup: Rachel has just joined the betting pool against everyone
jokes.punchline: Ross also wants to bet — moral outrage abandoned entirely for the sake of the action — and Monica realizes she's now the house against three people
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the betting joke — Ross's hypocrisy (moral outrage → 'can I get some of that?') is funny. Monica's realization she's bet against everyone is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We should probably keep Joey's tap dancing a secret. If word gets out that he's taking lessons, his tough guy image is done for.

jokes.text: Then there was the second set. The infamous 'booger' headshots.
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler are calculating how much Joey owes for headshots
jokes.punchline: 'The infamous booger headshots' — a casually dropped reference implying there exists a set of professional headshots in which Joey has a visible booger, famous enough to have an epithet
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and most characteristically Joey. The specificity of 'infamous booger headshots' is perfect — the word 'infamous' implies these are well-known within Joey's social circle, that this is a documented shameful episode in his career history. Only Joey would have a named category of failed headshots. Entirely original in this episode's context, perfectly economical, and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So you're telling me you paid three hundred dollars for accent lessons?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, and it's working! Listen to this.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Howdy, mon. I'm fixin' to get some jerk chicken, ya heard?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's a Jamaican-Southern hybrid.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a work in progress!

jokes.text: That's 500 and 500. That's... / You want a calculator? / Please.
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to add up how much money he owes Chandler; he gets stuck at 500+500
jokes.punchline: Joey can't add 500+500 and needs a calculator — Chandler's offer and Joey's immediate earnest 'Please' is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey dumb moment. The fact that he gets stuck at 500+500 (not some complex sum) is what makes it work. His earnest 'Please' for a calculator implies he knew he needed one and was relieved to be offered it. Character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, so I owe Chandler fifty bucks, right? Plus the twenty I borrowed last week... that's... seventy?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, no. Fifty plus twenty is... *presses calculator buttons repeatedly* ...how is it doing that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It keeps saying seventy! Why would it say that?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because fifty plus twenty equals seventy, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No it doesn't! It's fifty and twenty, not... *counts on fingers* ...Chandler, your calculator is broken.

jokes.text: Which we're still keeping under our hats. (re: tap classes)
jokes.setup: Chandler is listing Joey's acting training expenses, including tap classes
jokes.punchline: Chandler's aside that the tap classes are still a secret — implying Joey is embarrassed by tap dancing and they have a standing agreement not to mention it
jokes.explanation: Economical character joke with a lovely world-building implication — these two have an ongoing secret about Joey's tap class shame. The specificity of 'still keeping under our hats' suggests this is an established gentleman's agreement, which is funnier than a one-time embarrassment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no! Don't touch your eyes! I'm serious, those peppers are really hot.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I learned that the hard way about five minutes ago.

jokes.text: That dialect coach who helped you with a Southern accent. Which, after 20 hours of lessons, still came out Jamaican.
jokes.setup: Chandler is cataloguing Joey's failed acting investments
jokes.punchline: Twenty hours of Southern accent coaching produced a Jamaican accent — a spectacularly wrong outcome that reveals Joey's total incapacity for dialect work
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The specificity is everything — not just 'it didn't work' but '20 hours of lessons still came out Jamaican.' The Southern/Jamaican confusion is a great specific comic choice (they're not even vaguely similar accents). The phrasing 'came out Jamaican' as if it's an involuntary result is perfect. Only Joey could achieve this level of dialect failure. Approaches the 8+ benchmark clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's hot.

jokes.text: What the hell are you talking about? / The South will rise again, man.
jokes.setup: Joey is indignant about Chandler's claim that his Southern accent came out Jamaican
jokes.punchline: Joey's defense of his Southern accent is the Civil War battle cry 'The South will rise again' — delivered presumably in his terrible attempt at a Southern accent, confirming everything Chandler said
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. 'The South will rise again, man' works on multiple layers: (1) it's the perfect Confederate cliché for Joey to use as his sample Southern phrase, (2) the 'man' at the end is classic Joey casual speech bleeding into what he thinks is an accent, (3) the audience can imagine the Jamaican delivery, (4) it functions as proof of Chandler's claim — this IS the Jamaican-Southern hybrid. The word 'man' is crucial — it makes the whole thing Joey's voice rather than a Southern character's voice. Exceptional economy, originality, and character integration. This is an 8+ joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Make love? Ross, what are you, a 1970s folk singer?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? It's a perfectly acceptable term for—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's creepy. Just say 'have sex' like a normal person.

jokes.text: So I'm writing you a check for... / So you fell asleep during my movie. Big deal, right? / How do you clear this thing?
jokes.setup: Joey is using a calculator to add up all the money he owes Chandler
jokes.punchline: The sum is apparently so large that Joey immediately pivots to minimizing the movie incident — then can't figure out how to clear the calculator
jokes.explanation: Excellent visual/structural joke. The sum being so catastrophically large that Joey immediately tries to renegotiate (the movie sleep incident = debt forgiven?) is perfect Joey logic. 'How do you clear this thing?' adds a great button — he can't even face the number. The audience never sees the total, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, so calling me feminine isn't an effective seduction technique?

jokes.text: I am feeling nothing.
jokes.setup: Rachel is visibly suffering from the jalapeño heat
jokes.punchline: Rachel denies feeling anything — an obvious lie delivered while clearly in extreme discomfort, suggesting stubbornness or denial
jokes.explanation: Simple irony joke — obviously lying through her pain. Works as a visual gag because the audience can see her suffering. The delivery probably sells it more than the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Come on, Ross. Just hit me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm like a ketchup bottle. Sometimes you just have to hit me to get what you want out.

jokes.text: Speaking of hot, watching you do that...really makes me want to have sex with you.
jokes.setup: Rachel is suffering through spicy peppers for labor induction; Ross pivots to the medical recommendation (sex)
jokes.punchline: Ross uses 'speaking of hot' as a transition — linking jalapeño heat to Rachel's (dubious) sexiness — a terrible but earnest seduction attempt
jokes.explanation: Ross's terrible attempt at seduction via wordplay is very Ross — he thinks he's being clever with 'speaking of hot' but it's transparently bad. The fact that the target is a heavily pregnant, jalapeño-suffering Rachel makes the attempted flirtation funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's like a ketchup bottle. You have to bang it on the bottom to get it to come.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's the dirtiest thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: We know it's gonna work. It's doctor-recommended.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to convince Rachel to have sex with him to induce labor
jokes.punchline: Ross uses the doctor's medical recommendation as a seduction technique — essentially 'doctor's orders' as a pick-up line
jokes.explanation: Ross treating a medical recommendation as seduction leverage is perfectly in character — he's so desperate and awkward he genuinely thinks 'it's doctor-recommended' is an effective line.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hey Ross, don't you think I look... sexy?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I was going to do this sultry walk, but I can't really see my feet anymore.

jokes.text: Make love? What are you, a girl?
jokes.setup: Ross says 'I'm not gonna make love to you so you'll go into labor'
jokes.punchline: Rachel mocks Ross for using the phrase 'make love' — implying it's too soft/romantic for the clinical transaction being proposed
jokes.explanation: Very sharp and specific. Rachel attacking Ross's vocabulary choice during a failed seduction is funny — the phrase 'make love' IS pompous in this context, and Rachel calling it out as effeminate is a good character moment for her pragmatic aggression.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're such an idiot, and I love you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not really how compliments work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, it's how I work, you moron.

jokes.text: Always a great way to get into a man's pants.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just mocked Ross for saying 'make love'
jokes.punchline: Ross acknowledges dryly that questioning a man's masculinity is not effective as a seduction technique
jokes.explanation: Ross's dry self-awareness is used well here — he knows Rachel's approach is working against her goal. Brief and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I thought jalapeños were supposed to be good for you!

jokes.text: You'll be performing a service. Think of me as a ketchup bottle. Sometimes you have to bang on the end of it to get it to come out.
jokes.setup: Rachel is trying to persuade Ross to have sex with her to induce labor
jokes.punchline: Rachel's ketchup bottle metaphor — she is the ketchup bottle, the baby is the ketchup, Ross needs to 'bang on the end' — an aggressively un-sexy framing that probably backfires
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The ketchup bottle metaphor is an absurdist masterpiece — Rachel commits to it completely, the analogy is both logical and completely un-sexy, and 'bang on the end of it to get it to come out' has an inadvertent crudeness that the audience recognizes before Rachel does. The image is vivid, specific, and entirely original. High originality and quotability — this is a classic Friends line.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I did it! I did it! The baby's coming!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, the doctor said it could happen any time now.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, but it happened NOW. After I did all those things!

jokes.text: I love when you talk dirty to me.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just used the ketchup bottle metaphor as a seduction pitch
jokes.punchline: Ross sarcastically calls the ketchup bottle speech 'dirty talk' — reframing the absurd metaphor as failed eroticism
jokes.explanation: Good callback — sarcastically labeling Rachel's ketchup metaphor as dirty talk acknowledges how badly it worked while getting an extra laugh out of the metaphor. Quick and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wow, you really know a lot about Rachel!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I pick up on things.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm putting fifty bucks on whatever you say next.

jokes.text: Oh, whoops. Oh, I seem to have dropped my fork. / Let me just bend over and get it.
jokes.setup: Having failed with the ketchup metaphor, Rachel escalates to physical seduction
jokes.punchline: Rachel drops her fork and attempts a seductive bend — but she is nine months pregnant and 'bending over' is both physically impossible and visually hilarious
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy. The 'dropped fork' seduction cliché applied to a nine-months-pregnant woman is inherently funny, and Rachel's commitment to it makes it funnier. This is primarily a visual joke — the audience seeing the attempt is the punchline. High impact.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'll bet twenty bucks the baby's a boy!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, we already know it's a girl.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, then I'll bet twenty bucks it's NOT a boy!

jokes.text: Okay, enough. This is not going to happen. / Come on, Ross. I'm miserable here. Come on, you started this, now you finish it! Come on, wuss. Make love to me.
jokes.setup: Ross refuses to have sex with Rachel to induce labor; Rachel escalates her argument
jokes.punchline: Rachel's argument ends with 'Come on, wuss. Make love to me' — the least erotic invitation imaginable, undermining her own cause completely with the insult
jokes.explanation: Rachel now uses 'make love' herself after mocking Ross for the same phrase — a perfect ironic callback. And she undermines her invitation with 'wuss,' making 'Come on, wuss. Make love to me' an all-time terrible seduction line. The contradiction is the joke. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: How on earth will you ever annoy me? / Oh, wait a minute, I know.
jokes.setup: Ross has gone silent as a sulk/protest after Rachel called him a wuss; Rachel sarcastically notes the silence
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, wait a minute, I know' — Rachel immediately finding a new way Ross annoys her, implying the list is endless and she barely needs to think
jokes.explanation: Good comic beat — the implied infinite list of Ross's annoyances is very funny in context. Rachel finding the next annoyance immediately (before we see what it is) suggests effortless creativity in finding fault.

jokes.text: You'd think the jalapeño would clear up your sinuses, but no! (Rachel starts deliberately sniffling loudly)
jokes.setup: Rachel has found a new way to annoy Ross in retaliation for his silent treatment
jokes.punchline: Rachel begins loudly, dramatically sniffling — using the jalapeño as an excuse for exaggerated sniffling to irritate Ross, escalating the war of annoyances
jokes.explanation: Rachel weaponizing sniffling as retaliation is a good physical escalation. The jalapeño callback makes it structurally earned. Primarily a performance/visual joke.

jokes.text: That's not enough... What are you doing? / I'm getting that baby out of you!
jokes.setup: Rachel's sniffling has reached maximum annoyance; we don't see what she does next
jokes.punchline: Rachel declares she is 'getting that baby out' — implying her actions have escalated from sniffling to something more extreme, and that Rachel is now actively trying to self-induce labor through sheer irritation
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Rachel's self-torture (now actively trying to annoy herself into labor) is a good comic beat. The audience doesn't see what she does, making 'I'm getting that baby out of you!' funnier as an ambiguous battle cry.

jokes.text: Oh, God! / I know. / Oh, no, no, no. / I think my water just broke. / I am good!
jokes.setup: Rachel has been trying everything to induce labor; she erupts in another exclamation
jokes.punchline: Rachel's water breaks — and Ross's triumphant 'I am good!' implies he takes personal credit for the water breaking, as if his presence/actions caused it
jokes.explanation: Ross's 'I am good!' is the perfect button — his self-satisfaction about something he had no control over is very Ross. The timing (the moment after the water breaks) makes it land perfectly. Good character specificity.

jokes.text: Two hundred. / Thank you. / That's it. I don't care when the baby comes. No more betting.
jokes.setup: Monica has been losing bets all episode; Phoebe collects again
jokes.punchline: Monica dramatically quits the betting — but the phrasing 'I don't care when the baby comes' is hilariously indifferent to Rachel's actual wellbeing, centered entirely on Monica's financial losses
jokes.explanation: Monica's 'I don't care when the baby comes' as a declaration of betting retirement is perfectly self-centered — the baby's arrival is framed as a financial event rather than a human one. Good character work.

jokes.text: I guess we could bet one more time. / Is Rachel having the baby? / How did you know that?
jokes.setup: Monica has just sworn off betting; phone rings with news
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately reverses her vow when there's new betting opportunity — taking one phone call to abandon her resolution
jokes.explanation: Quick and effective callback — the irony of Monica's resolution lasting approximately 18 seconds is well-timed. 'I guess we could bet one more time' is the perfect weak-willed reversal.

jokes.text: I bet you the baby is over 7 pounds. / I bet you it has hair! / I bet you it's a girl. / We know it's a girl. / I'll give you really good odds.
jokes.setup: Everyone rushes to the hospital; the betting immediately resumes and escalates
jokes.punchline: Joey bets on something everyone already knows (it's a girl), and when corrected, tries to get action by offering 'really good odds' — implying he'll take the losing side just to stay in the game
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing escalation. Joey's 'I'll give you really good odds' on a known outcome is both dumb and weirdly strategic — he wants to participate more than he wants to win. Great Joey character moment to close out the episode.

tmdb_overview: Monica and Phoebe bet on when Rachel's baby will be born as the due date comes and goes as Rachel becomes extremely irritable. Meanwhile, Joey invites Chandler to his big movie premiere and he manages to fall asleep during it. Also, Ross attempts to help Rachel speed things along by trying every possible method suggested by the doctor, except one.
insight: Rachel's labor crisis sustains tension across 65 jokes, but emotional weight outpaces comedic payoff.
